title: What Happens to Your Investments in a Market Downturn?
summary: This guide explains what happens to your investments during a market downturn and how long-term investors respond.
body_markdown:
**In short:** In a downturn, the value of your investments falls on paper, but a paper loss only becomes a real loss if you sell. Market corrections and crashes are a normal part of investing, and markets have historically recovered from them over time, though that is never guaranteed. The costliest mistake is panic-selling. This is general information, not advice.


There is a particular kind of dread that comes with opening your investing app during a market slump and seeing red across the board. Your portfolio is worth less than it was last week, the headlines are grim, and every instinct is telling you to do something, anything, to stop the bleeding.


This guide is about that moment. It explains what actually happens to your investments when the market falls, why markets fall in the first place, what history tells us about downturns, and how experienced long-term investors think their way through them. It is general information, not investment advice. For the closely related question of when it does and does not make sense to sell, our guide on[when to sell a stock](https://learn.investbamboo.com/when-should-you-sell-a-stock-you-own/) is the companion to this one, and our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) covers the basics.


## What happens to your investments when the market falls?


When the market falls, the value of your holdings drops, but on paper rather than in your pocket. Until you sell, that loss is unrealised: it is a number on a screen, not money that has actually left you. This distinction is the single most important thing to understand about a downturn, and we return to it below because it changes everything about how you should respond.


Downturns are also normal. They are not a sign that investing is broken or that you made a mistake. They are a recurring feature of every stock market that has ever existed, and part of the price of the long-term returns that investing can offer.


## Correction, crash, or bear market: what is the difference?


These words get used loosely, but they have specific meanings. A **correction** is a fall of between 10% and 20% from a recent peak. A **bear market** is a deeper, more sustained fall of 20% or more. A **crash** is a sudden, sharp drop over a very short period, often days.


The important context is how ordinary the milder versions are. In developed markets, corrections have historically happened roughly every one to two years, and smaller pullbacks of 5% or more happen several times in a typical year. In other words, if you invest for any meaningful length of time, you will live through many downturns. Treating each one as a crisis is both exhausting and, as the rest of this guide argues, usually counterproductive.


## Why do markets fall?


Markets fall for a wide range of reasons, and often the fall has little to do with the specific companies you own. Common triggers include shifts in investor sentiment, profit-taking after a strong run, rising interest rates, disappointing economic data, political uncertainty, and global shocks that ripple across all markets at once.


Nigeria’s own market saw this in 2026. When the NGX pulled back that year, much of the selling was profit-taking and portfolio rebalancing rather than a sign that the underlying businesses had gone bad. As[Nairametrics reported at the time](https://nairametrics.com/2026/06/27/ngx-correction-why-smart-investors-arent-panicking/) , disciplined investors stayed focused on the quality of the companies they owned and the long-term value those investments could generate, while others panicked at the falling prices. The lesson is that a falling market is frequently a change in mood and money flows, not a verdict on the companies underneath.


## Paper losses versus real losses


A drop in your portfolio’s value is a paper loss, and it only becomes a real, permanent loss if you sell into the fall. This is why panic-selling is the genuine danger of a downturn, far more than the downturn itself.


Think about what selling in a slump actually does. It converts a temporary, on-paper decline into a locked-in, realised loss, and it takes you out of the market just before any potential recovery. Investors who sell in fear during a fall often miss the rebound and end up worse off than if they had done nothing at all. The market can recover while their money sits on the sidelines, and by the time they feel confident enough to return, much of the recovery has already happened.


The flip side is quietly reassuring. If you do not sell, a paper loss is exactly that: paper. Your shares still represent the same ownership in the same businesses they did before the price fell. Nothing about the companies has changed just because the quoted price has.


## Have markets recovered from downturns before?


Historically, markets have recovered from downturns over time, including severe ones, though this is a pattern from the past and not a guarantee about the future. It is worth being precise about that caveat, because no one can promise a recovery or say when it will come.


With that firmly in mind, the historical record is genuinely reassuring. In developed markets, corrections have often recovered within months, while deeper crashes have taken longer, and recoveries have rewarded investors who stayed the course. As[Fidelity has noted](https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/corrections) , while occasional downturns are unsettling, markets have historically recovered even from steep pullbacks, and most sound long-term strategies are built to withstand that volatility. The recovery from the sharp COVID-era fall in early 2020, for example, came unusually fast. The Nigerian market, like others, has fallen and then recovered through past cycles too.


None of this means every downturn recovers quickly, or that a given market must recover at all. It means that reacting to a fall as though it is permanent has, historically, been the wrong call for long-term investors. Time in the market has tended to matter more than timing it.


## What should you do in a downturn?


The most useful responses in a downturn are mostly about not doing the damaging things, and they are general principles rather than advice for your specific situation. A few consistently help.


Resist the urge to panic-sell. Before doing anything, ask whether the businesses you own have genuinely changed or whether only the price has. If it is only the price, that is usually a reason to wait, not to act. Revisit your original plan rather than the day’s headlines, since the plan was made calmly and the headlines are designed to alarm. Make sure you have an emergency fund elsewhere, so you are never forced to sell investments at a bad moment to cover a bill. And keep your time horizon in view: if you did not need this money for years, a bad few months does not change that.


Some long-term investors go further and see downturns as a chance to buy quality companies at lower prices. That view has logic to it, but it comes with a real caveat: no one knows whether prices will fall further before they rise, so this is a matter of individual judgement and risk tolerance, not a rule to follow blindly. Whatever you decide, it should follow from a plan, not from emotion in the moment.


## Why diversification matters most in a downturn


Diversification is the tool that makes downturns survivable, because spreading your money across different companies, sectors, and even currencies means no single fall can sink everything you own. When one part of your portfolio is down, another may be holding up, which cushions the overall blow and makes it easier to stay calm and stay invested.

Diversification does not remove risk or guarantee against losses, but it is the most reliable way to reduce the impact of any single market event.


## Frequently asked questions


**What happens to my money when the stock market falls?** The value of your holdings drops, but on paper. Until you sell, it is an unrealised loss, not money that has actually left you. Your shares still represent the same ownership in the same companies as before the price fell.


**Should I sell my investments during a market downturn?** Usually not, if nothing has changed about the companies you own. Selling into a fall converts a paper loss into a real one and risks missing the recovery. Ask whether the business has changed or only the price, and if only the price, waiting is often wiser.


**What is the difference between a correction and a bear market?** A correction is a fall of 10% to 20% from a recent peak and is usually shorter-lived. A bear market is a deeper fall of 20% or more that typically lasts longer. Both are normal parts of investing.


**Do markets always recover?** Historically, markets have recovered from downturns over time, including severe ones, and staying invested has tended to reward long-term investors. But this is a pattern from the past, not a guarantee. No one can promise a recovery or predict its timing.


**How can I protect my portfolio from downturns?** You cannot avoid downturns, but you can reduce their impact by diversifying across companies, sectors, and currencies, keeping an emergency fund so you are not forced to sell, and holding a long-term view so short-term falls do not drive your decisions.
